back: Functional: what a user can do ('create a short link'). Non-functional: a measurable property while doing it ('under 50 ms at p99').

front: What makes a latency requirement well formed?
back: A target, a percentile and where it is measured: 'first page under 300 ms at p99, at our servers'.
A rule that must hold in every state, e.g. never sell a seat twice, charge exactly once, one active trip per driver. Write each on its own line.
Users, scale, read/write mix, latency, consistency, durability, regions. Plus traffic shape, freshness, external limits, failure behaviour.

front: Test for whether to ask a clarifying question?
back: Would any answer change the design? If not, skip it or state an assumption.

front: Which questions first, if time is short?
back: Scale, read/write mix, the main latency target, then the one probing the likely invariant (consistency or durability).
1M arrivals in 60 s ≈ 16,700/s for 50,000 seats, 20 people per seat → waiting room and short holds.

front: Ride sharing: the real write load?
back: 1M drivers ÷ 4 s per GPS update = 250,000 location writes/s at peak, far more than trips.

front: Why ask about durability ('when is it done?')
back: It sets the acknowledgement point: e.g. chat's one tick means a replicated durable write before the ack.
'I'll assume X because Y; tell me if you have a different number.' Then write it on the board as A1, A2...

front: Three properties of a good assumption?
back: Round, conservative where it matters (higher peak, stricter invariant), and reversible.

front: When must you ask instead of assume?
back: When the assumption would remove the hard part of the problem, or would change the architecture and cannot be guessed safely.
Keep the core loop plus the requirement that makes the problem hard; park the rest on a written out-of-scope list.
'I'm leaving out X because it doesn't touch Y. Happy to come back to it.' Reason plus offer.

front: Three ways scope cutting goes wrong?
back: Cutting the hard part, cutting without saying so, and keeping a familiar nice-to-have that eats the time.

front: Recovery line when a new fact breaks an assumption?
back: 'That changes my assumption about X. Let me revise: the bottleneck is now Y, so I'll change Z.'
